citation.title: Estimating Average Causal Effects Under General Interference, with Application to a Social Network Experiment

standing_assumptions:
[Population and design: pp. 1914–1915 (PDF pp. 3–4)] Formally, suppose we have a finite population $U$ of units indexed by $i = 1, \ldots, N$ on which a randomized experiment is performed. Define a treatment assignment vector, $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, \ldots, z_N)'$, where $z_i \in \{1, \ldots, M\}$ specifies which of $M$ possible treatment values that unit $i$ receives. An experimental design contains a plan for randomly selecting a particular value of $\mathbf{z}$ from the $M^N$ different possibilities with predetermined probability $p_{\mathbf{z}}$. Restricting our attention only to treatment assignments that can be generated by a given experimental design, define $\Omega = \{\mathbf{z} : p_{\mathbf{z}} > 0\}$ so that $\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1, \ldots, Z_N)'$ is a random vector with support $\Omega$ and $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = p_{\mathbf{z}}$. Our analysis below focuses on the case where the design is known in the following sense: $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z})$ for all $\mathbf{z} \in \Omega$ is known. [Exposure mapping: p. 1915 (PDF p. 4)] We define an exposure mapping as a function that maps an assignment vector and unit-specific traits to an exposure value: $f : \Omega 	imes \Theta 	o \Delta$, where $	heta_i \in \Theta$ quantifies relevant traits of unit $i$. [Exposures and exposure probabilities: p. 1916 (PDF p. 5)] Define the exposure that unit $i$ receives as $D_i = f(\mathbf{Z}, 	heta_i)$, a random variable with support $\Delta_i \subseteq \Delta$ and for which $\Pr(D_i = d) = \pi_i(d)$. Note that because $|\Delta| \le |\Omega| 	imes N$, $\Delta$ is a finite set of $K \le |\Omega| 	imes N$ values, such that $\Delta = \{d_1, \ldots, d_K\}$. Then for each unit, $i$, we have a vector of probabilities, $(\pi_i(d_1), \ldots, \pi_i(d_K))' =  oldsymbol{\pi}_i$. [...] We have $\pi_i(d_k) = \sum_{\mathbf{z} \in \Omega} \mathbf{I}(f(\mathbf{z}, 	heta_i) = d_k)\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = \sum_{\mathbf{z} \in \Omega} p_{\mathbf{z}}\mathbf{I}(f(\mathbf{z}, 	heta_i) = d_k)$. [...] we define $\pi_{ij}(d_k)$ as the probability of the joint event that both units $i$ and $j$ are subject to exposure $d_k$, and we define $\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l)$ as the probability of the joint event that units $i$ and $j$ are subject to exposures $d_k$ and $d_l$, respectively. [Probability matrices: p. 1917 (PDF p. 6)] $\mathbf{I}_k\mathbf{P}\mathbf{I}_k'$ is an $N 	imes N$ symmetric matrix with individual exposure probabilities, the $\pi_i(d_k)$'s, on the diagonal and joint exposure probabilities, the $\pi_{ij}(d_k)$'s, on the off-diagonals. The nonsymmetric $N 	imes N$ matrix $\mathbf{I}_k\mathbf{P}\mathbf{I}_l'$, with zero diagonal and off-diagonal entries $\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l)$, yields all joint probabilities across exposure conditions $k$ and $l$. The zeroes on the diagonal are due to the fact that a unit cannot be subject to multiple exposure conditions at once. [Positivity: p. 1918 (PDF p. 7)] Suppose all units have nonzero probabilities of being subject to each of the $K$ exposures: $0 < \pi_i(d_k) < 1$ for all $i$ and $k$. [Potential outcomes: p. 1918 (PDF p. 7)] In the most general terms, each $\mathbf{z} \in \Omega$ can generate a potential outcome for unit $i$. We label the randomization potential outcome of unit $i$ associated with $\mathbf{z}$ as $y_i^r(\mathbf{z})$. These randomization potential outcomes are fixed for all units in the population and do not depend on the value of randomized treatment, $\mathbf{Z}$. CONDITION 1 (Properly specified exposure mapping). For all $i \in \{1, \ldots, N\}$ and $\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{z}' \in \Omega$ such that $f(\mathbf{z}, 	heta_i) = f(\mathbf{z}', 	heta_i)$, $y_i^r(\mathbf{z}) = y_i^r(\mathbf{z}')$. Given Condition 1, each unit $i$ has $|\Delta| = K$ potential outcomes, which we can write in terms of the exposure conditions as $(y_i(d_1), \ldots, y_i(d_K))$, where $y_i(d_k) = y_i^r(\mathbf{z})$, $ orall i \in \{1, \ldots, N\}$, $k \in \{1, \ldots, K\}$, and $\mathbf{z} \in \Omega$ such that $f(\mathbf{z}, 	heta_i) = d_k$. Let $Y_i$ be the observed outcome for unit $i$. CONDITION 2 (Consistent potential outcomes). $Y_i = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) y_i(d_k)$, $ orall i \in \{1, \ldots, N\}$. [p. 1919 (PDF p. 8)] Throughout, unless otherwise noted, we will be assuming Conditions 1 and 2. [Estimands: p. 1919 (PDF p. 8)] We seek estimates for all $k$ of $\mu(d_k) =  rac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_k) =  rac{1}{N} y^T(d_k)$, where $y^T(d_k)$ is the total of the potential outcomes under $d_k$. This allows us to define an average causal effect of being in exposure condition $d_k$ as compared to being in condition $d_l$ as $	au(d_k, d_l) =  rac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_k) -  rac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_l)$. [Estimators: pp. 1919–1920 (PDF pp. 8–9)] (1) $\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) rac{Y_i}{\pi_i(d_k)}$. $\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k) = (1/N)\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)$, with variance $\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k)) = (1/N^2)\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)]$. (3) $\widehat{	au_{HT}}(d_k, d_l) = \widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k) - \widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_l) =  rac{1}{N}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k) - \widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_l)]$, which is an estimator of $	au(d_k, d_l) =  rac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}[y_i(d_k) - y_i(d_l)]$, the average unit-level causal effect of exposure $k$ versus exposure $l$. [Exact probabilities: p. 1920 (PDF p. 9)] from here on our analysis assumes that we are working with $\mathbf{I}_k\mathbf{P}\mathbf{I}_k'$ and $\mathbf{I}_k\mathbf{P}\mathbf{I}_l'$ [the exact exposure probabilities; the simulated probabilities $\widehat{\pi}_i(d_k)$ enter only Propositions 3.1 and 4.1]. [Variance and covariance estimators of Section 5, used by several targets: pp. 1921–1924 (PDF pp. 10–13)] Given $\pi_{ij}(d_k) > 0$ for all $i, j$, the Horvitz–Thompson estimator for $\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)]$ is (7) $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)] = \sum_{i \in U} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)[1 - \pi_i(d_k)] \left[ rac{Y_i}{\pi_i(d_k)}ight]^2 + \sum_{i \in U}\sum_{j \in U \setminus i} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)\mathbf{I}(D_j = d_k) 	imes  rac{\pi_{ij}(d_k) - \pi_i(d_k)\pi_j(d_k)}{\pi_{ij}(d_k)}  rac{Y_i}{\pi_i(d_k)}  rac{Y_j}{\pi_j(d_k)}$. [p. 1922 (PDF p. 11)] (This notation requires that we define $0/0 = 0$.) [p. 1922] $\widehat{A_2}(d_k) = \sum_{i \in U}\sum_{j \in \{U \setminus i : \pi_{ij}(d_k) = 0\}} \left[ rac{\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) Y_i^2}{2\pi_i(d_k)} +  rac{\mathbf{I}(D_j = d_k) Y_j^2}{2\pi_j(d_k)}ight]$, noting that $\widehat{A_2}(d_k) = 0$ if $\pi_{ij}(d_k) > 0$ for all $i, j$. [p. 1923 (PDF p. 12)] For the case where $\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l) > 0$ for all $i, j$ such that $i 
e j$, we propose the Horvitz–Thompson-type estimator for the covariance (8) $\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k), \widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_l)] = \sum_{i \in U}\sum_{j \in U \setminus i} \left[ rac{\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)\mathbf{I}(D_j = d_l)}{\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l)}  rac{Y_i}{\pi_i(d_k)}  rac{Y_j}{\pi_j(d_l)} 	imes [\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l) - \pi_i(d_k)\pi_j(d_l)]ight] - \sum_{i \in U}\left[ rac{\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) Y_i^2}{2\pi_i(d_k)} +  rac{\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_l) Y_i^2}{2\pi_i(d_l)}ight]$. [p. 1924 (PDF p. 13)] a more general estimator for the covariance (10) $\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}_A}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k), \widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_l)] = \sum_{i \in U}\sum_{j \in \{U \setminus i : \pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l) > 0\}} \left[ rac{\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)\mathbf{I}(D_j = d_l)}{\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l)}  rac{Y_i}{\pi_i(d_k)}  rac{Y_j}{\pi_j(d_l)} 	imes [\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l) - \pi_i(d_k)\pi_j(d_l)]ight] - \sum_{i \in U}\sum_{j \in \{U : \pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l) = 0\}} \left[ rac{\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) Y_i^2}{2\pi_i(d_k)} +  rac{\mathbf{I}(D_j = d_l) Y_j^2}{2\pi_j(d_l)}ight]$. [p. 1924] we obtain a conservative variance estimator for $\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{	au_{HT}}(d_k, d_l))$ as (11) $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{	au_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)] =  rac{1}{N^2}\{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)] + \widehat{A_2}(d_k) + \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_l)] + \widehat{A_2}(d_l) - 2\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}_A}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k), \widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_l)]\}$. [Asymptotic framework and the conditions of Section 6. These are not standing assumptions: they are transcribed here once because several targets invoke them, and a target carries one of them only where its statement names it.] [p. 1924 (PDF p. 13)] Consider a sequence of nested populations indexed by size $N$, $(U_N)$. To define a notion of asymptotic growth, we let $N$ tend to infinity, allowing for the experimental design to be reapplied anew to each $U_N$, subject to the conditions defined below. [p. 1925 (PDF p. 14)] CONDITION 3 (Boundedness of potential outcomes and exposure probabilities). Potential outcomes and exposure probabilities are bounded so that, for all values $i$ and $d_k$, $|y_i(d_k)| \le c_1 < \infty$ and $|1/\pi_i(d_k)| \le c_2 < \infty$. [p. 1925] Define a pairwise dependency indicator $g_{ij}$ such that if $g_{ij} = 0$, then $D_i \perp\!\!\!\perp D_j$, else let $g_{ij} = 1$. CONDITION 4 (Restrictions on pairwise dependence). $\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N} g_{ij} = o(N^2)$. [p. 1925, as printed] Define a binary dependency indicator $h_{ij}$ over all pairs $(i, j) \in \{1, 2, \ldots, N\} 	imes \{1, 2, \ldots, N\}$, where $h_{ij}$ satisfies the following: for any pair of disjoint sets $\Gamma_1$ and $\Gamma_2 \subseteq \{1, \ldots, N\}$ such that there exists no pair $(i, j)$ with $h_{ij} = 1$ and either (i) $i \in \Gamma_1$ and $j 
otin \Gamma_2$, (ii) $j \in \Gamma_1$ and $i 
otin \Gamma_2$, (iii) $i 
otin \Gamma_1$ and $j \in \Gamma_2$, or (iv) $j 
otin \Gamma_1$ and $i \in \Gamma_2$, $\{D_i, i \in \Gamma_1\}$ and $\{D_i, i \in \Gamma_2\}$ are independent. CONDITION 5 (Local dependence). There exists a finite constant $m$ such that, for all $U_N$, $i \in 1, \ldots, N$, $\sum_{j=1}^{N} h_{ij} \le m$. [p. 1926 (PDF p. 15)] CONDITION 6 (Nonzero limiting variance.). $N\,\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{	au_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)] \xrightarrow{p} c$, where $c > 0$. [Remarks for the formalizer, not printed in the paper] $\mathrm{E}$, $\mathrm{Var}$ and $\mathrm{Cov}$ are taken over the randomization distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$ on $\Omega$ with weights $p_{\mathbf{z}}$; the population, the traits $	heta_i$, the exposure mapping and the potential outcomes are fixed. $U \setminus i$ means $U \setminus \{i\}$. Each unit receives exactly one exposure, so $\sum_{k} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) = 1$, $\pi_{ii}(d_k) = \pi_i(d_k)$ and $\pi_{ii}(d_k, d_l) = 0$ for $d_k 
e d_l$. Wherever two exposures $d_k$, $d_l$ appear together (Proposition 4.2, expressions (6) and (8)–(11), Section 6) they are distinct. The left side of Condition 6 is a deterministic sequence, so the printed $\xrightarrow{p}$ is ordinary convergence. Appendix A.6 (p. 1942) writes $c_3$ for a bound on $|y_i(d_k)|/\pi_i(d_k)$, which Condition 3 gives with $c_3 = c_1c_2$.

canonical_claim.statement:
[p. 1923 (PDF p. 12)] PROPOSITION 5.3. If $\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l) > 0$ for all $i, j$ such that $i 
e j$, then $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k), \widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_l)]] \le \mathrm{Cov}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k), \widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_l)]$. PROPOSITION 5.4. If $\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l) > 0$ for all $i, j$ such that $i 
e j$ and for all $i \in U$, $y_i(d_l) = y_i(d_k)$, then $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k), \widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_l)]] = \mathrm{Cov}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k), \widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_l)]$. [p. 1924 (PDF p. 13)] PROPOSITION 5.5. $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}_A}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k), \widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_l)]] \le \mathrm{Cov}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k), \widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_l)]$. PROPOSITION 5.6. $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{	au_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]] \ge \mathrm{Var}[\widehat{	au_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]$. [Hypotheses: the standing assumptions (a known design, Conditions 1 and 2, $0 < \pi_i(d) < 1$ for $d \in \{d_k, d_l\}$, $d_k 
e d_l$) and the convention $0/0 = 0$. Propositions 5.5 and 5.6 carry no condition on the joint exposure probabilities.]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Expressions (7), (8), (10), (11) and $\widehat{A_2}$ are in the standing assumptions; in Propositions 5.3 and 5.4 $\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}$ is expression (8), in Proposition 5.5 $\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}_A}$ is expression (10), and in Proposition 5.6 $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]$ is expression (11). The true covariance is expression (6) and the true variance of the difference is expression (5) (P013-T13). [p. 1923 (PDF p. 12)] For the case where $\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l) = 0$ for some $i, j$ and $k, l$, we can refine the expression for the covariance given in (6) to (9) $\mathrm{Cov}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k), \widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_l)] = \sum_{i \in U}\sum_{j \in \{U \setminus i : \pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l) > 0\}}\left[\frac{y_i(d_k)}{\pi_i(d_k)}\frac{y_j(d_l)}{\pi_j(d_l)} \times [\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l) - \pi_i(d_k)\pi_j(d_l)]\right] - \sum_{i \in U}\sum_{j \in \{U : \pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l) = 0\}} y_i(d_k)y_j(d_l)$, where the term on the last line subsumes the term on the last line in expression (6). [p. 1924] The result [Proposition 5.6] follows from Proposition 5.2, Proposition 5.5, and the linearity of expectations.
canonical_claim.note: Exact finite-population statements, verified by both readers by exact enumeration with zero joint probabilities and signed outcomes; no error touches them. Expected values: the first sum of (8) or (10) has expectation equal to the first sum of (6) or (9); the correction terms have expectation $-\sum_i [y_i(d_k)^2 + y_i(d_l)^2]/2$ in (8) and $-\sum_i\sum_{j : \pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l) = 0} [y_i(d_k)^2 + y_j(d_l)^2]/2$ in (10), each at most the corresponding $-\sum y_i(d_k)y_j(d_l)$ by Young's inequality; in Proposition 5.4 the difference is $\sum_i [y_i(d_k) - y_i(d_l)]^2/2 = 0$. Two related items are not errors of these statements: a sentence on p. 1921 gives the covariance estimator's bias the wrong sign (P013-E009, a clarity note), and the sentence after Proposition 5.3 says “second line” of (8) for its last line (P013-N001, a misprinted line reference). Proposition 5.6 is a finite lemma of P013-T2.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 7: unbiasedness of the difference estimator, expressions (12)–(13), and the bias bound for the Hajek estimator, expression (15)
canonical_claim.statement: (a) [Difference estimator, p. 1927 (PDF p. 16), as printed] Assume an auxiliary covariate vector $\mathbf{x}_i$ is observed for each $i$. We have some predefined function $g(\mathbf{x}_i, \boldsymbol{\xi}_i(d_k)) \to \mathbb{R}$, where $\boldsymbol{\xi}_i$ is a parameter vector. Ideally $g(\cdot)$ is calibrated on auxiliary data to produce values that approximate $y_i(d_k)$. We assume $\mathrm{Cov}[g(\mathbf{x}_i, \boldsymbol{\xi}_i(d_k)), Z_i] = 0$ as a sufficient condition for unbiasedness. Define (12) $\widehat{y^T_G}(d_k) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)\frac{Y_i}{\pi_i(d_k)} - \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)\frac{g(\mathbf{x}_i, \boldsymbol{\xi}_i(d_k))}{\pi_i(d_k)} + \sum_{i=1}^{N} g(\mathbf{x}_i, \boldsymbol{\xi}_i(d_k))$, which is unbiased for $y^T(d_k)$ by $\mathrm{E}\left[-\sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)\frac{g(\mathbf{x}_i, \boldsymbol{\xi}_i(d_k))}{\pi_i(d_k)} + \sum_{i=1}^{N} g(\mathbf{x}_i, \boldsymbol{\xi}_i(d_k))\right] = 0$. Define $\varepsilon_i(d_k) = Y_i - g(\mathbf{x}_i, \boldsymbol{\xi}_i(d_k))$ for cases with $D_i = d_k$. Then, by substitution, (13) $\widehat{y^T_G}(d_k) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)\frac{\varepsilon_i(d_k)}{\pi_i(d_k)} + \sum_{i=1}^{N} g(\mathbf{x}_i, \boldsymbol{\xi}_i(d_k))$. (b) [Hajek estimator, pp. 1928–1929 (PDF pp. 17–18), as printed] The Hajek ratio estimator is (15) $\widehat{\mu_H}(d_k) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)\frac{Y_i}{\pi_i(d_k)}} {\sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)\frac{1}{\pi_i(d_k)}}$. Note that $\mathrm{E}[\sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)\frac{1}{\pi_i(d_k)}] = N$ so that the Hajek estimator is the ratio of two unbiased estimators. [...] By Hartley and Ross (1954) and Särndal, Swensson and Wretman (1992), page 176, $|\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mu_H}(d_k)] - \mu(d_k)| \le \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) \frac{1}{\pi_i(d_k)}\right)\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\mu_H}(d_k))}$. Under Conditions 3 and 4, both variances will converge to zero, and the bias ratio will converge to zero. [Statements to formalize: (a1) with the values $g_i = g(\mathbf{x}_i, \boldsymbol{\xi}_i(d_k))$ fixed real numbers (not depending on $\mathbf{Z}$), $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{y^T_G}(d_k)] = y^T(d_k)$, and (12) equals (13) for every assignment; (b1) $\mathrm{E}[\sum_i \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)/\pi_i(d_k)] = N$; (b2) the displayed bias bound, with the ratio (15) taken as $0$ when no unit has exposure $d_k$ (the convention $0/0 = 0$ of p. 1922).]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\pi_i(d_k)$, $D_i$, $Y_i$, $y^T(d_k)$, $\mu(d_k)$ and Conditions 1 and 2 are in the standing assumptions. $Z_i$ is unit $i$'s own treatment assignment. [p. 1927] Variance estimation proceeds as in Section 5 using $\varepsilon_i(d_k)$ in place of $y_i(d_k)$ as long as $g(\mathbf{x}_i, \boldsymbol{\xi}_i(d_k))$ is fixed. [p. 1922] (This notation requires that we define $0/0 = 0$.)
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: For (b2): with $W = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)/\pi_i(d_k)$ and $T = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)Y_i/\pi_i(d_k)$, one has $T = \widehat{\mu_H}(d_k)\,W$ for every assignment (including $W = 0$, where $T = 0$), $\mathrm{E}[W] = 1$ and $\mathrm{E}[T] = \mu(d_k)$, so $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mu_H}(d_k)] - \mu(d_k) = -\mathrm{Cov}(\widehat{\mu_H}(d_k), W)$, and the bound is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P013-H5 also says that efficiency can be improved at little cost; that part is not a mathematical statement and is not a target, and the last printed sentence of (b) (both variances and the bias ratio converge to zero under Conditions 3 and 4) is an asymptotic remark given without proof, transcribed for context only. Reading of (a): the section calls $g$ “predefined” and later “fixed”; with fixed predictions (12) is unbiased with no further condition, which is the statement (a1). The printed covariance condition $\mathrm{Cov}[g(\mathbf{x}_i, \boldsymbol{\xi}_i(d_k)), Z_i] = 0$ would not be sufficient if the predictions could vary with the assignment, because the bias of (12) is $-\sum_i \mathrm{Cov}[g_i, \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)]/\pi_i(d_k)$ and $D_i$ depends on other units' assignments; a sufficient condition for random predictions is $\mathrm{Cov}[g_i, \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)] = 0$. That point is P013-E004, rated a clarity note, not an error, so it has no corrected-statement target; the validator's two-unit example is in validate/P013-E004/. The location-invariance sentence after (13) is P013-E005 (a clarity note) and is not part of this target. P013-E015 (the Hajek ratio on the event that no unit has exposure $d_k$) was not confirmed: the $0/0 = 0$ convention covers it.

canonical_claim.location: p. 1929 (PDF p. 18); p. 1930 (PDF p. 19); proof in Appendix A.8, pp. 1943–1944 (PDF pp. 32–33)
canonical_claim.statement: [p. 1929 (PDF p. 18)] CONDITION 7 (Misspecification). There exists some $i \in \{1, \ldots, N\}$ and $\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{z}' \in \Omega$ such that $f(\mathbf{z}, \theta_i) = f(\mathbf{z}', \theta_i)$ and $y_i^r(\mathbf{z}) \ne y_i^r(\mathbf{z}')$. Then $Y_i = \sum_{\mathbf{z} \in \Omega} \mathbf{I}(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) y_i^r(\mathbf{z})$, $\forall i \in \{1, \ldots, N\}$. PROPOSITION 8.1. Define $\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)$ as above, but suppose Condition 7 instead of Conditions 1 and 2. Then (16) $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)] = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{\mathbf{z} : f(\mathbf{z}, \theta_i) = d_k} w_{i,\mathbf{z}}\,y_i^r(\mathbf{z})$, where $w_{i,\mathbf{z}} = p_{\mathbf{z}}/\pi_i(d_k)$. [p. 1930 (PDF p. 19)] COROLLARY 8.1. Under Condition 7, $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)] = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[\sum_{\mathbf{z} : f(\mathbf{z}, \theta_i) = d_k} w_{i,\mathbf{z}}\,y_i^r(\mathbf{z}) - \sum_{\mathbf{z}' : f(\mathbf{z}', \theta_i) = d_l} w_{i,\mathbf{z}'}\, y_i^r(\mathbf{z}')\right]$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The design, $\Omega$, $p_{\mathbf{z}}$, $f$, $\theta_i$, $D_i$, $\pi_i(d_k)$, the randomization potential outcomes $y_i^r(\mathbf{z})$ and expressions (1) and (3) are in the standing assumptions; Conditions 1 and 2 are not assumed here. [Appendix A.8, pp. 1943–1944 (PDF pp. 32–33)] The result follows from iterating expectations: $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)] = \mathrm{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)\frac{Y_i}{\pi_i(d_k)}\right] = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)}{\pi_i(d_k)}\mathrm{E}[Y_i \mid D_i = d_k]\right] = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathrm{E}[Y_i \mid D_i = d_k] = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{\sum_{\mathbf{z} : f(\mathbf{z}, \theta_i) = d_k} p_{\mathbf{z}}y_i^r(\mathbf{z})} {\sum_{\mathbf{z} : f(\mathbf{z}, \theta_i) = d_k} p_{\mathbf{z}}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{\mathbf{z} : f(\mathbf{z}, \theta_i) = d_k} \frac{p_{\mathbf{z}}}{\pi_i(d_k)}y_i^r(\mathbf{z})$.
canonical_claim.note: Exact finite-population statements; both readers re-derived (16) and no error touches them. The identity (16) uses only $Y_i = \sum_{\mathbf{z} \in \Omega} \mathbf{I}(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z})y_i^r(\mathbf{z})$ and $\pi_i(d_k) > 0$; the existence clause of Condition 7 describes the situation and is not needed for the identity, which also holds under Conditions 1 and 2. In Corollary 8.1 the weight in the second sum is $w_{i,\mathbf{z}'} = p_{\mathbf{z}'}/\pi_i(d_l)$: the paper defines $w_{i,\mathbf{z}}$ with $\pi_i(d_k)$ only and reuses the symbol (P013-N003, a clarity note); a formalization should take the weight for the exposure that the assignment induces, $p_{\mathbf{z}}/\pi_i(f(\mathbf{z}, \theta_i))$.

canonical_claim.location: p. 1926 (PDF p. 15); proof in Appendix A.7, p. 1943 (PDF p. 32)
canonical_claim.statement: [As printed, p. 1926 (PDF p. 15)] PROPOSITION 6.2. Given Conditions 3, 5, and 6, Wald-type intervals constructed as $\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l) \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]}$ will tend to cover $\tau_{HT}(d_k, d_l)$ at least $100(1 - \alpha)\%$ of the time for large $N$. [Hypotheses attached: Conditions 3, 5 (with the dependency indicator $h_{ij}$ as printed) and 6, all transcribed in the standing assumptions; Conditions 1 and 2; the sequence of nested populations of Section 6, p. 1924.]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Conditions 1–6, expressions (1), (3), (7), (10), (11) and $\widehat{A_2}$ are transcribed in the standing assumptions, with locations. [p. 1926 (PDF p. 15), the paper's gloss on Condition 5] Condition 5 is equivalent to assuming that dependencies across exposures can be represented by a dependency graph such that the maximal degree of each unit tends to be limited relative to $N$. Condition 5 will allow us to straightforwardly invoke a central limit theorem for random fields as derived via Stein's method [Chen and Shao (2004), Example 2.4.1]. [...] Finite $m$ ensures that our variance estimators will converge at a sufficiently fast rate. $\tau_{HT}(d_k, d_l)$ without a hat is not defined in the paper.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: [Steps of the printed proof, Appendix A.7, p. 1943 (PDF p. 32)] By Proposition 5.6, $\mathrm{E}[N\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]] \ge N\,\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]$. Denote $a_{ij}(D_i, D_j)$ as the sum of the elements in $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]$ that incorporate observations $i$ and $j$. Note that all $a_{ij}(D_i, D_j)$ are bounded above by some finite constant by Condition 3: $\mathrm{Var}[N\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]] \le N^{-2}\,\mathrm{Var}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N} h_{ij}a_{ij}(D_i, D_j)\right] = N^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N}\sum_{l=1}^{N} \mathrm{Cov}[h_{ij}a_{ij}(D_i, D_j), h_{kl}a_{kl}(D_k, D_l)]$. Note that $\mathrm{Cov}[h_{ij}a_{ij}(D_i, D_j), h_{kl}a_{kl}(D_k, D_l)] \ne 0$ if and only if $h_{ij} = 1$ and $h_{kl} = 1$, and either $h_{ik} = 1$, $h_{il} = 1$, $h_{jk} = 1$, or $h_{jl} = 1$. By Condition 5, given $m \ll N$, each of these four conditions is satisfied by fewer than $Nm^3$ of the elements of the quadruple summation, and the number of elements in their union is at most $4Nm^3$. Thus, $\mathrm{Var}[N\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]] = O(N^{-2} \times N) = O(N^{-1})$. [Of these, the expectation inequality and the count of at most $4Nm^3$ quadruples (for a symmetric $h$ with row sums at most $m$) are valid finite statements; the boundedness of $a_{ij}$ by Condition 3 and the resulting $O(N^{-1})$ bound are not (P013-T1), and “if and only if” holds only as “only if” (P013-E011, a clarity note).]
canonical_claim.note: The paper's asymptotic headline result on interval coverage; false as printed (P013-T1), corrected in P013-T2. The natural formal reading of “will tend to cover [...] at least $100(1 - \alpha)\%$ of the time for large $N$” is $\liminf_{N \to \infty} \Pr\{|\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l) - \tau(d_k, d_l)| \le z_{1-\alpha/2} \sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]}\} \ge 1 - \alpha$, with the coverage target $\tau(d_k, d_l)$ (P013-T9). Four findings touch the statement or its proof: P013-E001 (Moderate; missing control of the joint exposure probabilities), P013-E002 (Minor; the printed $h_{ij}$, P013-T5 and P013-T6), P013-E007 (Minor; limits that need not exist, P013-T7 and P013-T8) and P013-E012 (Minor; the undefined $\tau_{HT}$). State it as printed with the natural reading; it is not provable, and P013-T1 refutes it under both the printed and the corrected reading of Condition 5.

canonical_claim.location: p. 1925 (PDF p. 14); proof in Appendix A.6, p. 1942 (PDF p. 31)
canonical_claim.statement: [p. 1925 (PDF p. 14)] PROPOSITION 6.1. Given Conditions 3 and 4, $\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l) - \tau(d_k, d_l) \xrightarrow{p} 0$ as $N \to \infty$. [Hypotheses attached: Conditions 3 and 4 (standing assumptions, p. 1925), Conditions 1 and 2, and the sequence of nested populations of Section 6 (p. 1924), with the design reapplied to each $U_N$; the constants $c_1, c_2$ of Condition 3 do not depend on $N$, and Condition 4 is an order condition along the sequence.]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Conditions 3 and 4, the pairwise dependency indicator $g_{ij}$, expressions (1) and (3) and $\tau(d_k, d_l)$ are in the standing assumptions. $\xrightarrow{p}$ is convergence in probability under the randomization distributions of the designs on $U_N$: for every $\epsilon > 0$, $\Pr(|\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l) - \tau(d_k, d_l)| > \epsilon) \to 0$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: [Appendix A.6, p. 1942 (PDF p. 31)] $\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k)$ is unbiased for $\mu(d_k)$, and thus we need only consider the variance. Condition 3 implies that, for all values $i$ and $d_k$, $|y_i(d_k)|/\pi_i(d_k) \le c_3 < \infty$. Substituting from equation (2), $N^2\,\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k)) \le c_3^2N + c_3^2\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N} g_{ij}$. [These are exact for each fixed $N$, as is Chebyshev's inequality $\Pr(|\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k) - \mu(d_k)| > \epsilon) \le \mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k))/\epsilon^2$; and $\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l) - \tau(d_k, d_l) = [\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k) - \mu(d_k)] - [\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_l) - \mu(d_l)]$. The variance bound uses $\pi_i(d_k)[1 - \pi_i(d_k)] \le 1$, $|\pi_{ij}(d_k) - \pi_i(d_k)\pi_j(d_k)| \le 1$ and $\pi_{ij}(d_k) = \pi_i(d_k)\pi_j(d_k)$ when $g_{ij} = 0$.]
canonical_claim.note: Both readers followed Appendix A.6 and found the result to hold. The statement itself is printed with the correct target $\tau(d_k, d_l)$; its proof prints the centering target of the mean as $\mu_{HT}(d_k)$ (P013-E012; corrected in P013-T9, part (i)). The proof invokes “Slutsky's theorem” for the difference; the difference of two sequences that converge to zero in probability converges to zero in probability, which is all that is needed.
